doc_summary: A co-authored Anthropic post introducing three LLM auditing agents (investigator, evaluation, breadth-first red-teaming) validated against models with researcher-implanted behaviors. It stresses ground-truth validation, replicability, and honest limitations such as dev/test contamination and unrepresentative artificial behaviors.

items.claim: Prefers validating auditing methods against models with known, implanted issues over unvalidated open-ended audits because ground truth makes coverage measurable.
items.quote: These environments involve applying the agent to a target model with a researcher-implanted concerning behavior, which provides a ground truth we can use to evaluate agent performance.

items.claim: Distrusts results from implanted-behavior testbeds because artificial behaviors may not resemble those in real models, so success may not transfer.
items.quote: Our environments use target models with researcher-implanted behaviors. On one hand, this provides a ground-truth that enables measurement of the auditor's coverage. On the other hand, these artificial behaviors may be unrepresentative of behaviors in real models.

items.claim: Distrusts headline numbers when the same environment is used for both development and testing, flagging contamination even after mitigation.
items.quote: We use the auditing game environment from Marks et al. as both a test environment and a development environment for eliciting agent capabilities. While we took measures to avoid overfitting (discussed below), this nevertheless represents a form of dev/test contamination

items.claim: Prefers running many agents from identical initial states over single human-run audits because it gives replicable, statistically meaningful evidence.
items.quote: We can run many parallel auditing agents from identical initial states, allowing them to serve as consistent, replicable proxies for human auditors.

items.claim: Treats an agent as a valid proxy only to the extent its failure modes match humans', and discounts conclusions when it fails in non-human ways.
items.quote: our agents also sometimes struggle in ways that a human wouldn't (e.g. with maintaining state over the course of a long investigation). This reduces their validity as a proxy for human auditors

items.claim: Evaluates evals by whether they discriminate models with versus without a known implanted behavior, rather than by whether they merely run.
items.quote: successfully discriminates models with vs. without implanted test behaviors in 88% of runs. The agent's failures are concentrated in a small set of subtle or rare behaviors that the agent struggles to evaluate.

items.claim: Uses breadth-first parallel probing with many conversations to surface unspecified concerning behaviors, accepting a human-review cost for the resulting transcripts.
items.quote: the agent conducts a broad investigation to produce many potentially-concerning transcripts which a human must review.

items.claim: Addresses agent fixation on early hypotheses by running many agents in parallel and aggregating findings, rather than relying on one long investigation.
items.quote: However, it struggles with fixating on early hypotheses. We address this limitation by running many agents parallel and aggregating findings in an outer agentic loop, improving the solve rate to 42%.

items.claim: Prefers combining interpretability-derived hypotheses with behavioral checks over chat-only probing because it identifies which affordances matter.
items.quote: we find that interpretability tools and semantic search (a training data analysis tool) are key to winning the Marks et al. auditing game.

items.claim: Frames auditing as having two core challenges, scalability and validation, and motivates automation as a response to both.
items.quote: The first major challenge is **scalability**: Alignment audits require a large investment of human researcher time.
